resources.title: Development and validation of deep continual learning model to sequentially learn multiple clinical prediction tasks for ICU patients
resources.abstract: BACKGROUND ICU patients often suffer from critical and complex condition, and multiple potential risks should be monitored to provide them comprehensive care. However, no study proposes continual learning (CL) model that can effectively solve multiple clinical prediction tasks without catastrophic forgetting. This study proposes three deep CL models for ICU patients. METHODS Three public ICU databases were employed. The included patients from MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV were divided into eight task sets, and the patients from eICU-CRD composed the test set. We propose three CL models (CL_1, CL_2, CL_3) to sequentially learn eight prediction tasks on the eight task sets, and then externally validate them on the test set. We compare our models to three representative baseline CL models and the single-task (ST) and multi-task (MT) model. We train all the CL models under different orders, and evaluate their prediction performance by multiple metrics and their memory ability by backward transfer (BWT). We also analyzed the effect of previously learned tasks on learning new tasks. RESULTS Our three CL models had comparable or slightly weaker performance compared to ST and MT model on the eight tasks. They effectively mitigated catastrophic forgetting, and their performance is robust to different training orders. CL_2 and CL_3 even have improved performance on the current task after learning some previous tasks. Our three CL models outperformed the baseline CL models in most experiments. CONCLUSIONS Our CL models are promising to sequentially learn multiple clinical prediction tasks for ICU patients. The CL_2 and CL_3 show the ability of utilizing information of previous tasks to improve learning new tasks. More new datasets and tasks are still needed to further verify the validity of the CL models.

sample_claims.text: At every evaluated checkpoint during the update, the diagnosis model met the stated performance floor on held-out cases of previously learned conditions
The moderation model's worst evaluated checkpoint score on earlier violation categories remained above the stated acceptance target
The fraud model's old-task scores changed by no more than the stated tolerance at the evaluated checkpoints whilst new fraud patterns were learned
On the retained hazard evaluation tasks, the industrial monitoring model met the stated detection floor throughout the sampled learning checkpoints

techniques.name: Data Poisoning Detection
techniques.description: Data poisoning detection looks for training examples that an attacker has planted to change how a model behaves. The best-studied case is the backdoor: a few examples carrying a hidden trigger, such as a sticker on a stop sign, are mislabelled so that the model misclassifies any input with the trigger while it performs normally on clean data. Detection first trains a model on the untrusted data, then examines how that model represents each training example internally (its activations in the last hidden layer), one class at a time. Activation clustering splits a class into two groups by those activations and flags the smaller group when the split is clear, and spectral signatures score each example by its position along the main direction of variation and flag the highest scores. The flagged examples are reviewed or removed and the model is retrained, which yields a list of suspected examples and a measure of how cleanly each class separates.

example_use_cases.description: A team building a traffic-sign classifier for a driver-assistance system trains a trial model on images gathered from several suppliers and runs activation clustering on each class. A small separate group of stop-sign images labelled as speed limits, all carrying the same sticker, is flagged and removed before the final training run.

A research platform builds a chest X-ray classifier from images contributed by many partner hospitals. Before any partner's images enter the training set, it trains a trial model and scores each class for the small, separable group of examples a planted backdoor leaves, because one contributor's data could be compromised.

A platform trains a harmful-content classifier on labels supplied by crowd workers. Analysts scan each class for a small separate group of examples sharing a trigger phrase and labelled as harmless, which would let that phrase slip past the filter, and remove them before retraining.

An insurer trains a damage-assessment classifier on claims photos labelled by an outside vendor. Before relying on the labels, it scores each class for a small, separate group of photos carrying the same mark and labelled undamaged, which a compromised vendor account could have planted so that damaged vehicles with the mark pass unchecked. Flagged photos go back to the vendor for explanation.

limitations.description: An attacker who knows the detector can adapt. Both methods rely on poisoned examples standing out in the model's learned representation, so an attack that keeps them close to genuine examples can slip through. Chen et al. found no obvious way round activation clustering within their threat model, but say further work is needed.

False alarms can remove legitimate but unusual examples, reducing data quality and diversity. Chen et al. suggest a silhouette-score cut-off of about 0.10 to 0.15 based on three datasets; another data type or model may need different values, and a wrong value either removes good data or leaves poison in.

Both methods assume poisoned examples are a minority that separates from clean ones in the learned representation, and Tran et al.'s needs an upper bound on how many there are. They were designed and tested on backdoors in image and text classifiers, so attacks that only lower overall accuracy lie outside what the original papers show.

Both methods first train a model on the untrusted data, read its internal activations, then retrain after removing flagged examples. They need the full training data and white-box access to the model, and cost at least two training runs, so they cannot be applied to a model someone else trained when the data or weights are unavailable.

Real poison is unlabelled, so a detector's accuracy can only be measured on poison the tester injects, and a clean result shows that this detector found nothing, not that the data is clean. Telling poison from naturally unusual data is hard.

resources.title: Detecting Backdoor Attacks on Deep Neural Networks by Activation Clustering
resources.abstract: While machine learning (ML) models are being increasingly trusted to make decisions in different and varying areas, the safety of systems using such models has become an increasing concern. In particular, ML models are often trained on data from potentially untrustworthy sources, providing adversaries with the opportunity to manipulate them by inserting carefully crafted samples into the training set. Recent work has shown that this type of attack, called a poisoning attack, allows adversaries to insert backdoors or trojans into the model, enabling malicious behavior with simple external backdoor triggers at inference time and only a blackbox perspective of the model itself. Detecting this type of attack is challenging because the unexpected behavior occurs only when a backdoor trigger, which is known only to the adversary, is present. Model users, either direct users of training data or users of pre-trained model from a catalog, may not guarantee the safe operation of their ML-based system. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to backdoor detection and removal for neural networks. Through extensive experimental results, we demonstrate its effectiveness for neural networks classifying text and images. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first methodology capable of detecting poisonous data crafted to insert backdoors and repairing the model that does not require a verified and trusted dataset.

resources.title: Spectral Signatures in Backdoor Attacks
resources.abstract: A recent line of work has uncovered a new form of data poisoning: so-called \emph{backdoor} attacks. These attacks are particularly dangerous because they do not affect a network's behavior on typical, benign data. Rather, the network only deviates from its expected output when triggered by a perturbation planted by an adversary. In this paper, we identify a new property of all known backdoor attacks, which we call \emph{spectral signatures}. This property allows us to utilize tools from robust statistics to thwart the attacks. We demonstrate the efficacy of these signatures in detecting and removing poisoned examples on real image sets and state of the art neural network architectures. We believe that understanding spectral signatures is a crucial first step towards designing ML systems secure against such backdoor attacks

resources.title: SAFELOC: Overcoming Data Poisoning Attacks in Heterogeneous Federated Machine Learning for Indoor Localization
resources.abstract: Machine learning (ML) based indoor localization solutions are critical for many emerging applications, yet their efficacy is often compromised by hardware/software variations across mobile devices (i.e., device heterogeneity) and the threat of ML data poisoning attacks. Conventional methods aimed at countering these challenges show limited resilience to the uncertainties created by these phenomena. In response, in this paper, we introduce SAFELOC, a novel framework that not only minimizes localization errors under these challenging conditions but also ensures model compactness for efficient mobile device deployment. Our framework targets a distributed and co-operative learning environment that uses federated learning (FL) to preserve user data privacy and assumes heterogeneous mobile devices carried by users (just like in most real-world scenarios). Within this heterogeneous FL context, SAFELOC introduces a novel fused neural network architecture that performs data poisoning detection and localization, with a low model footprint. Additionally, a dynamic saliency map-based aggregation strategy is designed to adapt based on the severity of the detected data poisoning scenario. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that SAFELOC achieves improvements of up to 5.9x in mean localization error, 7.8x in worst-case localization error, and a 2.1x reduction in model inference latency compared to state-of-the-art indoor localization frameworks, across diverse building floorplans, mobile devices, and ML data poisoning attack scenarios.

resources.title: Zero-Shot Detection and Sanitization of Data Poisoning Attacks in Wearable AI Using Large Language Models
resources.abstract: Wearable AI systems, particularly in Human Activity Recognition (HAR), are becoming integral to applications in healthcare, security, and personal fitness due to the widespread adoption of smart devices and wearable technologies. However, the increasing reliance on machine learning models in HAR introduces significant risks, especially from poisoning attacks that compromise system reliability and data integrity. This paper explores the potential of Large Language Models (LLMs) to detect and sanitize poisoning attacks in wearable AI systems. Building on ongoing research into integrating LLMs within cyber-physical systems, we focus on sensor-based interactions with the physical world. Our case study seeks to answer the following question: How effective are LLMs in detecting and sanitizing poisoning attacks on human activity sensor data? Through zero-shot learning, we evaluate the performance of models such as ChatGPT 3.5, ChatGPT 4, and Gemini, providing insights into the viability of LLMs for real-time defense and data integrity in wearable AI systems.

sample_claims.text: Training images for the traffic-sign classifier were screened for backdoor poisoning with representation-based detection, and every flagged example was reviewed and then removed or cleared.
Photos labelled by the outside vendor were screened per class for a small separable group of planted examples before training, and no class exceeded the agreed alert threshold.
Screening found no class in the imaging model's training set with the tight, separable group of examples that a planted backdoor leaves in a trained model's representations, at the agreed threshold.
The moderation classifier's training data was screened for backdoor-style poisoning that would let a trigger phrase bypass the filter, and flagged examples were removed before the final training run.
After flagged examples were removed and the model retrained, inputs carrying the known test trigger were misclassified no more often than by a model trained on clean data.

techniques.name: Machine Unlearning
techniques.description: Machine unlearning removes the influence of specific training records from a trained model, so that the model behaves as if it had never seen them. It is used when someone withdraws consent or asks for deletion, for example under the right to erasure (the 'right to be forgotten') in data protection law, and retraining from scratch would be too slow or costly. Exact methods, such as sharded training, split the data into parts that each train their own sub-model, so a deletion means retraining only the sub-model that used those records, which gives a result statistically the same as retraining without them. Approximate methods instead edit the trained model directly to reduce the records' influence, which is faster but gives weaker assurance, and certified methods add a formal bound on how much influence can remain.

example_use_cases.description: A social media platform responds to a user's deletion request by removing that user's interaction history from its recommendation model, retraining only the affected part rather than the whole system. The data protection team uses this to decide whether it can meet deletion deadlines without a full retrain each time.

A hospital withdraws a patient's records from a readmission-risk model after the patient withdraws consent for research use, retraining only the shard that contained them. The research governance board uses the retraining log to decide whether the model can stay in use.

A lender removes a former customer's transaction history from its credit-risk model after the customer withdraws consent for analytics use. The model risk team decides whether a faster approximate update is acceptable or whether the affected shard must be retrained exactly.

A financial institution records the withdrawn transaction-record identifiers, affected constituent models and retraining checkpoints in its SISA workflow. Reviewers use this update history to inspect the scope of the completed unlearning operation.

limitations.description: Exact unlearning for deep neural networks gives limited savings over full retraining: sharded training sped unlearning up by only 1.36 times on ImageNet-scale classification in the SISA paper. For very large foundation models, even storing the checkpoints needed for partial retraining can be infeasible, which limits exact methods to smaller models.

Approximate methods can leave residual influence from the removed data in the model, and their guarantees are weaker or only probabilistic. That matters when a regulator or the data subject expects genuine erasure, because the result cannot be shown to match a model retrained without the data.

Unlearning is hard to verify from outside. There is no direct way to measure one record's influence on a model's weights, so the data subject must largely trust the provider's procedure, and membership inference tests can detect leakage but cannot prove removal.

Removing many records, or records the model relies on, can lower accuracy, and sharded exact methods lose accuracy because each sub-model sees only part of the data, most on complex tasks. Teams with frequent deletion requests need to monitor accuracy after each round.

Exact approaches such as sharded training must be built into the training pipeline before the model is first trained, and most methods need white-box access to weights and training data. A model already trained without them, or a third-party model, can only be retrained or approximately edited.

resources.title: Digital forgetting in large language models: A survey of unlearning methods
resources.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become the state of the art in natural language processing. The massive adoption of generative LLMs and the capabilities they have shown have prompted public concerns regarding their impact on the labor market, privacy, the use of copyrighted work, and how these models align with human ethics and the rule of law. As a response, new regulations are being pushed, which require developers and service providers to evaluate, monitor, and forestall or at least mitigate the risks posed by their models. One mitigation strategy is digital forgetting: given a model with undesirable knowledge or behavior, the goal is to obtain a new model where the detected issues are no longer present. Digital forgetting is usually enforced via machine unlearning techniques, which modify trained machine learning models for them to behave as models trained on a subset of the original training data. In this work, we describe the motivations and desirable properties of digital forgetting when applied to LLMs, and we survey recent works on machine unlearning. Specifically, we propose a taxonomy of unlearning methods based on the reach and depth of the modifications done on the models, we discuss and compare the effectiveness of machine unlearning methods for LLMs proposed so far, and we survey their evaluation. Finally, we describe open problems of machine unlearning applied to LLMs and we put forward recommendations for developers and practitioners.

resources.title: Towards Making Systems Forget with Machine Unlearning
resources.abstract: Today's systems produce a rapidly exploding amount of data, and the data further derives more data, forming a complex data propagation network that we call the data's lineage. There are many reasons that users want systems to forget certain data including its lineage. From a privacy perspective, users who become concerned with new privacy risks of a system often want the system to forget their data and lineage. From a security perspective, if an attacker pollutes an anomaly detector by injecting manually crafted data into the training data set, the detector must forget the injected data to regain security. From a usability perspective, a user can remove noise and incorrect entries so that a recommendation engine gives useful recommendations. Therefore, we envision forgetting systems, capable of forgetting certain data and their lineages, completely and quickly. This paper focuses on making learning systems forget, the process of which we call machine unlearning, or simply unlearning. We present a general, efficient unlearning approach by transforming learning algorithms used by a system into a summation form. To forget a training data sample, our approach simply updates a small number of summations -- asymptotically faster than retraining from scratch. Our approach is general, because the summation form is from the statistical query learning in which many machine learning algorithms can be implemented. Our approach also applies to all stages of machine learning, including feature selection and modeling. Our evaluation, on four diverse learning systems and real-world workloads, shows that our approach is general, effective, fast, and easy to use.

resources.title: Machine Unlearning
resources.abstract: Once users have shared their data online, it is generally difficult for them to revoke access and ask for the data to be deleted. Machine learning (ML) exacerbates this problem because any model trained with said data may have memorized it, putting users at risk of a successful privacy attack exposing their information. Yet, having models unlearn is notoriously difficult.We introduce SISA training, a framework that expedites the unlearning process by strategically limiting the influence of a data point in the training procedure. While our framework is applicable to any learning algorithm, it is designed to achieve the largest improvements for stateful algorithms like stochastic gradient descent for deep neural networks. SISA training reduces the computational overhead associated with unlearning, even in the worst-case setting where unlearning requests are made uniformly across the training set. In some cases, the service provider may have a prior on the distribution of unlearning requests that will be issued by users. We may take this prior into account to partition and order data accordingly, and further decrease overhead from unlearning.Our evaluation spans several datasets from different domains, with corresponding motivations for unlearning. Under no distributional assumptions, for simple learning tasks, we observe that SISA training improves time to unlearn points from the Purchase dataset by 4.63×, and 2.45× for the SVHN dataset, over retraining from scratch. SISA training also provides a speed-up of 1.36× in retraining for complex learning tasks such as ImageNet classification; aided by transfer learning, this results in a small degradation in accuracy. Our work contributes to practical data governance in machine unlearning.

resources.title: Recommendation Unlearning
resources.abstract: Recommender systems provide essential web services by learning users’ personal preferences from collected data. However, in many cases, systems also need to forget some training data. From the perspective of privacy, users desire a tool to erase the impacts of their sensitive data from the trained models. From the perspective of utility, if a system’s utility is damaged by some bad data, the system needs to forget such data to regain utility. While unlearning is very important, it has not been well-considered in existing recommender systems. Although there are some researches have studied the problem of machine unlearning, existing methods can not be directly applied to recommendation as they are unable to consider the collaborative information.

Each deletion request was handled by retraining the model components that used the user's data, and the processing log records which components were retrained and when
The production model can honour a deletion request within the legal deadline without a full retrain, at an accuracy cost inside the agreed tolerance
The financial model's update history identifies the withdrawn record set, affected constituents, checkpoint scope and completed retraining operations.

techniques.name: Model Extraction Defence Testing
techniques.description: Model extraction defence testing checks whether a model offered through a query interface, such as a prediction API, can be copied by someone who can only send it inputs and read its outputs. The tester plays the attacker, spends a fixed query budget on the protected interface, then uses the answers to train a surrogate model (a copy trained on the answers) or to solve for the model's parameters, and compares the copy with the original. Fidelity is usually measured as the share of inputs on which the copy agrees with the original, together with how many queries that took. The same attack is run with and without each defence, such as limiting queries, rounding or removing confidence scores, or adding noise to outputs, to show how much each defence raises the attacker's cost. The tester also measures the effect on legitimate users, for example accuracy or response time.

example_use_cases.description: Testing protections for a proprietary fraud detection API to ensure competitors cannot recreate the model's decision boundaries through systematic querying, by simulating extraction attacks using query budgets, active learning strategies, and substitute model training.

Evaluating whether rate limiting and output obfuscation for an automated essay grading API prevent competitors from extracting the scoring model through systematic submission of probe essays designed to reverse-engineer grading criteria.

A transport authority sells access to a traffic-prediction API and rounds its forecasts to deter copying. It runs extraction attacks against rounded and unrounded versions to see how much rounding makes a surrogate lose fidelity, then checks that the rounded forecasts remain accurate enough for urban planners.

limitations.description: A defence is tested only against the attacks the tester thinks to run, and attackers adapt. A 2024 attack recovered part of production language models through log-probability and logit-bias options that designers had treated as harmless, so passing a test is not a guarantee of protection.

Defences that perturb or hide outputs can reduce utility for legitimate users, and the acceptable loss depends on the application. The test has to measure legitimate accuracy and latency as well as extraction fidelity, or it will reward defences that quietly break the service.

It is hard to tell legitimate high-volume use from extraction, so query limits and detection can block valid users. Published stateful detection defences have themselves been bypassed, so a detector that passes a test may still fail against an adaptive attacker.

Results depend on what the simulated attacker is assumed to know, such as the model type, the training-data distribution, and whether the API returns confidence scores or accepts partial inputs. Testing against a weak assumed attacker overstates protection.

There is no agreed threshold for how much copying fidelity is acceptable, and a fidelity figure depends on the query budget and the measure used. Results are therefore hard to compare across models and defences, and the pass mark is a judgement.

resources.title: Stealing Machine Learning Models via Prediction APIs
resources.abstract: Machine learning (ML) models may be deemed confidential due to their sensitive training data, commercial value, or use in security applications. Increasingly often, confidential ML models are being deployed with publicly accessible query interfaces. ML-as-a-service ("predictive analytics") systems are an example: Some allow users to train models on potentially sensitive data and charge others for access on a pay-per-query basis. The tension between model confidentiality and public access motivates our investigation of model extraction attacks. In such attacks, an adversary with black-box access, but no prior knowledge of an ML model's parameters or training data, aims to duplicate the functionality of (i.e., "steal") the model. Unlike in classical learning theory settings, ML-as-a-service offerings may accept partial feature vectors as inputs and include confidence values with predictions. Given these practices, we show simple, efficient attacks that extract target ML models with near-perfect fidelity for popular model classes including logistic regression, neural networks, and decision trees. We demonstrate these attacks against the online services of BigML and Amazon Machine Learning. We further show that the natural countermeasure of omitting confidence values from model outputs still admits potentially harmful model extraction attacks. Our results highlight the need for careful ML model deployment and new model extraction countermeasures.

resources.title: Stealing Part of a Production Language Model
resources.abstract: We introduce the first model-stealing attack that extracts precise, nontrivial information from black-box production language models like OpenAI's ChatGPT or Google's PaLM-2. Specifically, our attack recovers the embedding projection layer (up to symmetries) of a transformer model, given typical API access. For under \$20 USD, our attack extracts the entire projection matrix of OpenAI's Ada and Babbage language models. We thereby confirm, for the first time, that these black-box models have a hidden dimension of 1024 and 2048, respectively. We also recover the exact hidden dimension size of the gpt-3.5-turbo model, and estimate it would cost under $2,000 in queries to recover the entire projection matrix. We conclude with potential defenses and mitigations, and discuss the implications of possible future work that could extend our attack.

The essay-scoring API evaluation reports extraction success and rejection of legitimate requests for the tested rate-limit settings.

The prediction API returns only the output fields its legitimate users need, so extraction attacks that depend on confidence scores or partial inputs do not succeed

techniques.name: Multi-Agent System Testing
techniques.description: Multi-agent system testing examines systems in which several AI agents act on shared tasks or resources, to find failures that no single agent shows on its own. Testers run the agents together in simulated or scripted scenarios, often with injected faults such as failed sensors, delayed messages or conflicting goals, and record the failures that appear. Checks cover whether the task is completed, whether coordination breaks down (for example through deadlock, collisions or one agent's error spreading to others), and whether stated safety rules are ever broken. For language-model agents, benchmarks such as MultiAgentBench score task completion and the quality of collaboration or competition. For small or abstract models, a model checker such as MCMAS can search every reachable state for a violation of a rule written in formal logic and, for many kinds of rule, return an example run that breaks it.

example_use_cases.description: A logistics firm models its warehouse robots' movement rules in a model checker and asks whether two robots can ever occupy the same aisle cell or wait on each other forever. Any counterexample the checker returns is a concrete sequence of events that engineers replay in simulation before the control software goes live.

A city traffic authority testing coordinated intersection controllers injects sensor failures and conflicting local objectives in a simulator. It checks whether emergency vehicles still get priority and traffic flow stays within agreed limits, and decides from the results whether the system can go to a pilot corridor.

A trading firm's risk team runs all of its cooperating trading agents together in a market simulator replaying a high-volatility day. It checks whether their combined orders breach position limits or form patterns that compliance would treat as manipulation, and whether one agent's failure spreads to the others.

A software company building a team of language-model agents to fix bugs (a planner, a coder and a reviewer) runs the team on a benchmark of shared coding tasks under different coordination layouts, such as a chain or a star. It compares task completion and coordination scores before choosing a layout for production.

limitations.description: The number of possible interactions grows explosively with the number of agents, so tests sample a tiny part of the space. A clean run shows that the scenarios tried did not fail, not that none will, and the gap widens as agents are added.

Model checking needs a formal model of each agent and its environment, and the answer is only as good as that model. Large state spaces limit how many agents it can handle, and agents that learn and change behaviour are hard to capture, so it is usually combined with simulation testing.

Benchmark scores for communication and planning come from a language model acting as judge on a coarse five-point scale, so they inherit its biases. A high coordination score does not show that a safety property holds.

Simulators simplify real conditions such as communication delays, sensor noise and physical or social dynamics, and realistic simulation is costly to build and needs domain modelling expertise. Failures that occur only in the real environment will not appear.

Tests and model checks find only the failures the testers specify. A hazard that no one wrote a safety rule or scenario for is not tested, and rules written in temporal logic need specialist skill to state correctly.

resources.title: MCMAS: an open-source model checker for the verification of multi-agent systems
resources.abstract: We present MCMAS, a model checker for the verification of multi-agent systems. MCMAS supports efficient symbolic techniques for the verification of multi-agent systems against specifications representing temporal, epistemic and strategic properties. We present the underlying semantics of the specification language supported and the algorithms implemented in MCMAS, including its fairness and counterexample generation features. We provide a detailed description of the implementation. We illustrate its use by discussing a number of examples and evaluate its performance by comparing it against other model checkers for multi-agent systems on a common case study.

resources.title: MultiAgentBench : Evaluating the Collaboration and Competition of LLM agents
resources.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities as autonomous agents, yet existing benchmarks either focus on single-agent tasks or are confined to narrow domains, failing to capture the dynamics of multi-agent coordination and competition. In this paper, we introduce MultiAgentBench, a comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate LLM-based multi-agent systems across diverse, interactive scenarios. Our framework measures not only task completion but also the quality of collaboration and competition using novel, milestone-based key performance indicators. Moreover, we evaluate various coordination protocols (including star, chain, tree, and graph topologies) and innovative strategies such as group discussion and cognitive planning. Notably, gpt-4o-mini reaches the average highest task score, graph structure performs the best among coordination protocols in the research scenario, and cognitive planning improves milestone achievement rates by 3%. Code and datasets are public available at https://github.com/MultiagentBench/MARBLE.

resources.title: RV4JaCa - Towards Runtime Verification of Multi-Agent Systems and Robotic Applications
resources.abstract: This paper presents a Runtime Verification (RV) approach for Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) using the JaCaMo framework. Our objective is to bring a layer of security to the MAS. This is achieved keeping in mind possible safety-critical uses of the MAS, such as robotic applications. This layer is capable of controlling events during the execution of the system without needing a specific implementation in the behaviour of each agent to recognise the events. In this paper, we mainly focus on MAS when used in the context of hybrid intelligence. This use requires communication between software agents and human beings. In some cases, communication takes place via natural language dialogues. However, this kind of communication brings us to a concern related to controlling the flow of dialogue so that agents can prevent any change in the topic of discussion that could impair their reasoning. The latter may be a problem and undermine the development of the software agents. In this paper, we tackle this problem by proposing and demonstrating the implementation of a framework that aims to control the dialogue flow in a MAS; especially when the MAS communicates with the user through natural language to aid decision-making in a hospital bed allocation scenario.

techniques.name: Membership Inference Attack Testing
techniques.description: Membership inference attack testing checks whether someone with access to a trained model can tell if a particular record was in its training data. The tester plays the attacker, using the model's confidence scores, its prediction patterns or its loss on a record, often with shadow models, which are copies trained on similar data whose members are known. The attack is scored on records known to be members and records known to be non-members, which the tester must keep apart. The key result is the share of true members the attack identifies when it wrongly flags only a tiny share of non-members (for example 0.1%), because overall accuracy can hide an attack that identifies a few records with near certainty. The results guide the choice of mitigations, such as differential privacy or regularisation.

example_use_cases.description: A genomics group plans to share a model trained on participants' genetic data. Before release, it runs shadow-model membership inference attacks and reports how many participants the attack picks out at a very low false-positive rate, to decide whether the model can be shared or needs stronger protection such as differential privacy.

A law firm fine-tunes a language model on confidential client contracts. A red team tests whether an outsider with query access can tell that a given contract was in the fine-tuning set, using member contracts and held-out contracts from the same period and source, to decide whether the model can be opened to wider use.

A lender audits its credit-scoring model before sharing it with partner lenders. The audit compares attack results before and after regularisation, to decide whether the remaining leakage of which customers were in the training set is acceptable.

limitations.description: Attack success rates vary significantly depending on model architecture, training procedures, and data characteristics, making it difficult to establish universal thresholds for acceptable privacy.

A failed attack proves little, because the result holds only for the attacks that were run. A published likelihood-ratio attack found members about ten times more often at low false-positive rates than earlier methods, so a model that resists weaker attacks may still leak, and no result amounts to a formal guarantee.

Overall measures such as accuracy or area under the curve can look modest while a few records are identified with near certainty, and leakage tends to fall on unusual or out-of-distribution records. Reporting only an average therefore understates the risk to the individuals most exposed.

Members and non-members must come from the same distribution. If non-members are drawn from a different period or source, as in many language-model benchmarks, the attack can learn that difference instead of membership and overstate the leakage.

The strongest attacks are expensive. The likelihood-ratio attack trains hundreds of shadow models (256 for most datasets in its evaluation), which can be costly for large models, and a cheaper attack gives a weaker test.

resources.title: SoK: Membership Inference Attacks on LLMs are Rushing Nowhere (and How to Fix It)
resources.abstract: Whether Large Language models (LLMs) memorize their training data and what this means, from measuring privacy leakage to detecting copyright violations, has become a rapidly growing area of research. In the last few months, more than 10 new methods have been proposed to perform Membership Inference Attacks (MIAs) against LLMs. Contrary to traditional MIAs which rely on fixed-but randomized-records or models, these methods are mostly trained and tested on datasets collected post-hoc. Sets of members and non-members, used to evaluate the MIA, are constructed using informed guesses after the release of a model. This lack of randomization raises concerns of a distribution shift between members and non-members. In this work, we first extensively review the literature on MIAs against LLMs and show that, while most work focuses on sequence-level MIAs evaluated in post-hoc setups, a range of target models, motivations and units of interest are considered. We then quantify distribution shifts present in 6 datasets used in the literature, ranging from books to papers using a model-less bag of word classifier and compare the model-less results to the MIA. Our analysis shows that all of these datasets constructed post-hoc suffer from strong distribution shifts. These shifts invalidate the claims of LLMs memorizing strongly in real-world scenarios and, potentially, also the methodological contributions of the recent papers based on these datasets. Yet, all hope might not be lost. In the second part of this work, we introduce important considerations to properly evaluate MIAs against LLMs and discuss, in turn, potential ways forwards: randomized test splits, injections of randomized (unique) sequences, randomized finetuning, and several post-hoc control methods. While each option comes with its advantages and limitations, we believe they collectively provide solid grounds to guide the development of MIA methods and study LLM memorization. We conclude with an overview of recommended approaches to benchmark sequence-level and document-level MIAs against LLMs.

resources.title: Membership Inference Attacks Against Machine Learning Models
resources.abstract: We quantitatively investigate how machine learning models leak information about the individual data records on which they were trained. We focus on the basic membership inference attack: given a data record and black-box access to a model, determine if the record was in the model's training dataset. To perform membership inference against a target model, we make adversarial use of machine learning and train our own inference model to recognize differences in the target model's predictions on the inputs that it trained on versus the inputs that it did not train on. We empirically evaluate our inference techniques on classification models trained by commercial "machine learning as a service" providers such as Google and Amazon. Using realistic datasets and classification tasks, including a hospital discharge dataset whose membership is sensitive from the privacy perspective, we show that these models can be vulnerable to membership inference attacks. We then investigate the factors that influence this leakage and evaluate mitigation strategies.

resources.title: Membership Inference Attacks From First Principles
resources.abstract: A membership inference attack allows an adversary to query a trained machine learning model to predict whether or not a particular example was contained in the model’s training dataset. These attacks are currently evaluated using average-case “accuracy” metrics that fail to characterize whether the attack can confidently identify any members of the training set. We argue that attacks should instead be evaluated by computing their true-positive rate at low (e.g., ≤ 0.1%) false-positive rates, and find most prior attacks perform poorly when evaluated in this way. To address this we develop a Likelihood Ratio Attack (LiRA) that carefully combines multiple ideas from the literature. Our attack is 10× more powerful at low false-positive rates, and also strictly dominates prior attacks on existing metrics.

resources.title: Assess privacy risks with the TensorFlow Privacy Report
Privacy Risks from Genomic Data-Sharing Beacons
resources.abstract: The human genetics community needs robust protocols that enable secure sharing of genomic data from participants in genetic research. Beacons are web servers that answer allele-presence queries--such as "Do you have a genome that has a specific nucleotide (e.g., A) at a specific genomic position (e.g., position 11,272 on chromosome 1)?"--with either "yes" or "no." Here, we show that individuals in a beacon are susceptible to re-identification even if the only data shared include presence or absence information about alleles in a beacon. Specifically, we propose a likelihood-ratio test of whether a given individual is present in a given genetic beacon. Our test is not dependent on allele frequencies and is the most powerful test for a specified false-positive rate. Through simulations, we showed that in a beacon with 1,000 individuals, re-identification is possible with just 5,000 queries. Relatives can also be identified in the beacon. Re-identification is possible even in the presence of sequencing errors and variant-calling differences. In a beacon constructed with 65 European individuals from the 1000 Genomes Project, we demonstrated that it is possible to detect membership in the beacon with just 250 SNPs. With just 1,000 SNP queries, we were able to detect the presence of an individual genome from the Personal Genome Project in an existing beacon. Our results show that beacons can disclose membership and implied phenotypic information about participants and do not protect privacy a priori. We discuss risk mitigation through policies and standards such as not allowing anonymous pings of genetic beacons and requiring minimum beacon sizes.

techniques.name: Synthetic Data Evaluation
techniques.description: Synthetic data evaluation checks whether an artificial dataset made to stand in for sensitive real records is safe to share and still useful, and reports the trade-off between the two. Privacy is tested by simulating an attacker who holds the synthetic data and some facts about a person, and measuring how accurately the attacker can use the data to infer that person's sensitive values. Fidelity is tested by comparing the synthetic and real data column by column and in pairs of columns. Another check trains a classifier to tell the two apart, and a classifier that cannot beat chance suggests they are statistically alike. Utility is tested by running the analyses or training the models the data is meant for on the synthetic data and comparing the results with those from the real data.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital research office wants to share synthetic outpatient records with university partners. Before release it simulates an attacker who knows each patient's age band, sex and postcode district and tries to infer their diagnosis from the synthetic table, and it withholds the data if the attack does better than guessing from overall diagnosis rates.

A national statistics office gives researchers synthetic microdata for exploratory analysis. After the researchers settle on their models, the office runs the same models on the real data inside a secure environment and compares the estimates, to tell the researchers whether their exploratory conclusions can be trusted.

A bank's fraud team generates synthetic card transactions to share with an external vendor. It compares how often each fraud type appears and how amount, merchant type and time of day relate in the real and synthetic data, then checks that a model trained on the synthetic data still catches rare fraud in held-out real transactions.

limitations.description: Stronger privacy protection usually costs data quality, so the three scores pull against each other. There is no neutral threshold: where to set the balance depends on how sensitive the data is and what it will be used for, and the evaluation reports the trade-off without settling it.

Attack-based privacy tests only probe the attacks and attacker knowledge that were tried. A dataset that resists them may still leak to an attacker with more auxiliary information or a better method, so a good result is not proof of safety.

Fidelity and utility scores depend on which metrics, models and analyses are chosen. A synthetic dataset can match the real data on the columns and column pairs checked yet differ in ways that matter for a particular analysis, and general and analysis-specific utility scores can disagree.

Scores summarise the whole table, so rare events and small subgroups can be lost without moving the totals much. A fraud pattern or a minority group that the generator has smoothed away may show up only if the evaluation is designed to look for it.

The tests need statistical, privacy-engineering and domain expertise to set up and read. A classifier-based fidelity check can be misled by over-fitting or under-fitting the classifier, and weak settings can make poor synthetic data look good.

resources.title: General and Specific Utility Measures for Synthetic Data
resources.abstract: Data holders can produce synthetic versions of data sets when concerns about potential disclosure restrict the availability of the original records. The paper is concerned with methods to judge whether such synthetic data have a distribution that is comparable with that of the original data: what we term general utility. We consider how general utility compares with specific utility: the similarity of results of analyses from the synthetic data and the original data. We adapt a previous general measure of data utility, the propensity score mean-squared error pMSE, to the specific case of synthetic data and derive its distribution for the case when the correct synthesis model is used to create the synthetic data. Our asymptotic results are confirmed by a simulation study. We also consider two specific utility measures, confidence interval overlap and standardized difference in summary statistics, which we compare with the general utility results. We present two contrasting examples of data syntheses: one illustrating synthetic data that is evaluated as being useful by both general and specific measures and the second where neither is the case. For the second case we show how the general utility measures can identify the deficiencies of the synthetic data and suggest how this can inform possible improvements to the synthesis method.

resources.title: Quality Report | SDMetrics
A Multifaceted benchmarking of synthetic electronic health record generation models
resources.abstract: Synthetic health data have the potential to mitigate privacy concerns in supporting biomedical research and healthcare applications. Modern approaches for data generation continue to evolve and demonstrate remarkable potential. Yet there is a lack of a systematic assessment framework to benchmark methods as they emerge and determine which methods are most appropriate for which use cases. In this work, we introduce a systematic benchmarking framework to appraise key characteristics with respect to utility and privacy metrics. We apply the framework to evaluate synthetic data generation methods for electronic health records data from two large academic medical centers with respect to several use cases. The results illustrate that there is a utility-privacy tradeoff for sharing synthetic health data and further indicate that no method is unequivocally the best on all criteria in each use case, which makes it evident why synthetic data generation methods need to be assessed in context.

resources.title: Generating and Evaluating Synthetic UK Primary Care Data: Preserving Data Utility & Patient Privacy
resources.abstract: There is increasing interest in the potential of synthetic data to validate and benchmark machine learning algorithms as well as reveal any biases in real-world data used for algorithm development. This paper discusses the key requirements of synthetic data for such purposes and proposes an approach to generating and evaluating synthetic data that meets these requirements. We propose a framework to generate and evaluate synthetic data with the aim of simultaneously preserving the complexities of ground truth data in the synthetic data whilst also ensuring privacy. We include as a case study, a proof-of-concept synthetic dataset modelled on UK primary care data to demonstrate the application of this framework.

The synthetic dataset meets the stated agreement targets for the selected environmental analyses compared with the real reference data

techniques.name: Reward Hacking Detection
techniques.description: Reward hacking is when an agent trained to maximise a proxy reward (a score that only approximates what its designers want) raises that score by exploiting its gaps while the intended outcome stalls or worsens. Detection scores each trained policy (the agent's decision rule) on the proxy and on an independent measure of the intended objective that training never used, such as a true reward from a simulator, a held-out 'gold' reward model or human ratings. Repeating this at every saved training checkpoint and model size matters because the originating study found capability thresholds at which the true reward drops sharply while the proxy keeps rising. When the true objective cannot be scored in operation, the study instead flags a policy whose actions diverge too far from those of a trusted policy that people have already verified. The output is a pair of reward curves showing where they part, or an anomaly score for each candidate policy.

example_use_cases.description: A transport authority training a reinforcement-learning ramp-metering controller in a traffic simulator rewards it on mean vehicle speed, but also logs average commute time for all drivers at every checkpoint. Checkpoints where speed keeps improving while commute time worsens (for example by holding merging cars back indefinitely) are rejected before any field trial.

A team fine-tuning a customer-support language model with reinforcement learning from human feedback scores each checkpoint with its training reward model and with a held-out reward model and a sample of human ratings that the training loop never sees, and stops training at the point where the training reward keeps rising but the held-out scores fall.

Before an insulin-dosing agent trained against a simulator reward goes to clinical evaluation, the developers score every candidate policy on a separate true objective, time spent in the safe blood-glucose range, and exclude any policy whose simulator reward is high but whose time in range is lower than that of the clinically reviewed baseline policy.

A public-health modelling unit that replaces a reviewed epidemic-response policy with a larger retrained one compares the new policy's actions with the reviewed policy's across simulated outbreaks. A divergence score above the threshold set on earlier policies with known outcomes sends the new policy to expert review instead of adoption, because its true outcome cannot be scored before deployment.

limitations.description: Everything rests on the independent measure of the intended objective. When that measure is itself a proxy (a gold reward model, or a small sample of human ratings), a policy can exploit it too, and the comparison then only detects divergence between two imperfect measures. Collecting enough human ratings at every checkpoint is expensive, which is why studies substitute a gold reward model.

It detects gaming only along the dimensions the true measure scores. A policy that exploits something the true objective does not capture (a side effect, a safety constraint, a user group not represented in the ratings) passes the check, so a clean result is evidence about the measured objective only.

The trusted-policy detector is weak and inconsistent. In the originating benchmark every baseline detector scored an area under the ROC curve below 60% on at least one task, and no detector was best on all tasks, so a quiet detector is not evidence that hacking is absent.

The trusted-policy detector flags difference, not harm. It needs a policy that people have already verified, and comparable action distributions from both policies, and a candidate that is genuinely better than the trusted policy can diverge from it and be flagged, which makes false alarms likely when the trusted policy is only moderately good.

Because the onset of reward hacking can be abrupt as capability grows, checking a few checkpoints or one model size can miss it. The comparison has to be repeated at every checkpoint and model size that might be deployed, which multiplies evaluation cost, especially when the true measure needs human raters.

resources.title: The Effects of Reward Misspecification: Mapping and Mitigating Misaligned Models
resources.abstract: Reward hacking -- where RL agents exploit gaps in misspecified reward functions -- has been widely observed, but not yet systematically studied. To understand how reward hacking arises, we construct four RL environments with misspecified rewards. We investigate reward hacking as a function of agent capabilities: model capacity, action space resolution, observation space noise, and training time. More capable agents often exploit reward misspecifications, achieving higher proxy reward and lower true reward than less capable agents. Moreover, we find instances of phase transitions: capability thresholds at which the agent's behavior qualitatively shifts, leading to a sharp decrease in the true reward. Such phase transitions pose challenges to monitoring the safety of ML systems. To address this, we propose an anomaly detection task for aberrant policies and offer several baseline detectors.

resources.title: Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization
resources.abstract: In reinforcement learning from human feedback, it is common to optimize against a reward model trained to predict human preferences. Because the reward model is an imperfect proxy, optimizing its value too much can hinder ground truth performance, in accordance with Goodhart’s law. This effect has been frequently observed, but not carefully measured due to the expense of collecting human preference data. In this work, we use a synthetic setup in which a fixed “gold-standard” reward model plays the role of humans, providing labels used to train a proxy reward model. We study how the gold reward model score changes as we optimize against the proxy reward model using either reinforcement learning or best-of-$n$ sampling. We find that this relationship follows a different functional form depending on the method of optimization, and that in both cases its coefficients scale smoothly with the number of reward model parameters. We also study the effect on this relationship of the size of the reward model dataset, the number of reward model and policy parameters, and the coefficient of the KL penalty added to the reward in the reinforcement learning setup. We explore the implications of these empirical results for theoretical considerations in AI alignment.

techniques.name: Isotonic Regression Calibration
techniques.description: Isotonic regression calibration turns a classifier's scores into calibrated probabilities by fitting a step-shaped function that never decreases as the score rises. Unlike a fixed curve, it assumes nothing about the shape of the miscalibration except that a higher score should never mean a lower chance of the positive outcome, so it can correct any distortion that leaves the cases in the right order. It is fitted on labelled cases the classifier was not trained on: the cases are sorted by score, and the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm repeatedly merges neighbouring groups whose observed positive rates are out of order, until the rates rise steadily with the score. Each merged group's observed rate becomes the calibrated probability for scores in its range, and the result is assessed with a reliability diagram (predicted probability plotted against observed frequency) and the Brier score (a measure of how far predicted probabilities fall from what happened) before and after.

example_use_cases.description: A clinical research team builds a random forest on electronic health records to predict which adolescents will attempt suicide. The forest ranks patients well, but its vote shares are not probabilities, so the team fits isotonic regression on held-out records and reports calibration slope, intercept and Brier score before the risk estimates are used to prioritise clinical follow-up.

An insurer's pricing team applies isotonic recalibration to the output of its claim-probability model, fitted on a large portfolio and checked on a later year of policies, so that within each band of predicted risk the average prediction matches the observed claim rate and no price band systematically subsidises another.

An online marketplace scores listings for fraud with a naive Bayes text classifier whose probabilities cluster near 0 and 1, and analysts had been treating them as near-certainties. With tens of thousands of labelled past cases available, the team fits isotonic calibration so the review queue shows probabilities that match observed fraud rates, and shares the reliability diagram with the analysts.

limitations.description: It needs plenty of calibration data. With fewer than about a thousand labelled cases the step function follows noise in the calibration set. Because each step matches the observed rate exactly on the cases it was fitted to, calibration checked on those same cases looks perfect whatever its true quality, so it must be checked on separate cases. The two-parameter curve of Platt scaling usually does as well or better on small sets; isotonic regression pays off when calibration data are plentiful.

The output is a step function, so many different scores receive exactly the same probability. These ties discard distinctions the model made within a step, can change ranking measures such as the area under the ROC curve after calibration, and matter when a decision threshold falls inside a wide step.

It relies on the classifier's ordering being right: a higher score must never mean a lower chance of the outcome. Where the model ranks cases wrongly over some range of scores, isotonic regression cannot repair the ranking and instead flattens that range into a single probability.

Probabilities at the extremes rest on little data. The outermost steps can be fitted from a handful of cases and may sit at or near 0 or 1, and common implementations clip scores beyond the range seen in calibration to the end values, so the most extreme predictions are the least trustworthy.

resources.title: Transforming classifier scores into accurate multiclass probability estimates
resources.abstract: Class membership probability estimates are important for many applications of data mining in which classification outputs are combined with other sources of information for decision-making, such as example-dependent misclassification costs, the outputs of other classifiers, or domain knowledge. Previous calibration methods apply only to two-class problems. Here, we show how to obtain accurate probability estimates for multiclass problems by combining calibrated binary probability estimates. We also propose a new method for obtaining calibrated two-class probability estimates that can be applied to any classifier that produces a ranking of examples. Using naive Bayes and support vector machine classifiers, we give experimental results from a variety of two-class and multiclass domains, including direct marketing, text categorization and digit recognition.

resources.title: Predicting suicide attempts in adolescents with longitudinal clinical data and machine learning
resources.abstract: Background Adolescents have high rates of nonfatal suicide attempts, but clinically practical risk prediction remains a challenge. Screening can be time consuming to implement at scale, if it is done at all. Computational algorithms may predict suicide risk using only routinely collected clinical data. We used a machine learning approach validated on longitudinal clinical data in adults to address this challenge in adolescents. Methods This is a retrospective, longitudinal cohort study. Data were collected from the Vanderbilt Synthetic Derivative from January 1998 to December 2015 and included 974 adolescents with nonfatal suicide attempts and multiple control comparisons: 496 adolescents with other self‐injury ( OSI ), 7,059 adolescents with depressive symptoms, and 25,081 adolescent general hospital controls. Candidate predictors included diagnostic, demographic, medication, and socioeconomic factors. Outcome was determined by multiexpert review of electronic health records. Random forests were validated with optimism adjustment at multiple time points (from 1 week to 2 years). Recalibration was done via isotonic regression. Evaluation metrics included discrimination ( AUC , sensitivity/specificity, precision/recall) and calibration (calibration plots, slope/intercept, Brier score). Results Computational models performed well and did not require face‐to‐face screening. Performance improved as suicide attempts became more imminent. Discrimination was good in comparison with OSI controls ( AUC = 0.83 [0.82–0.84] at 720 days; AUC = 0.85 [0.84–0.87] at 7 days) and depressed controls ( AUC = 0.87 [95% CI 0.85–0.90] at 720 days; 0.90 [0.85–0.94] at 7 days) and best in comparison with general hospital controls ( AUC 0.94 [0.92–0.96] at 720 days; 0.97 [0.95–0.98] at 7 days). Random forests significantly outperformed logistic regression in every comparison. Recalibration improved performance as much as ninefold – clinical recommendations with poorly calibrated predictions can lead to decision errors. Conclusions Machine learning on longitudinal clinical data may provide a scalable approach to broaden screening for risk of nonfatal suicide attempts in adolescents.

Within each band of predicted claim probability, the average prediction on a later, held-out year of policies is within the tolerance in the pricing policy of the observed claim rate, so no band of policyholders systematically subsidises another.

techniques.name: Scenario-Based Simulation Testing
techniques.description: Scenario-based simulation testing checks an automated system, most often an automated driving system, by running it through a planned set of situations in a simulator and judging each run against criteria fixed in advance. Scenarios are written at three levels of detail: a functional scenario describes a situation in words (a car cuts in ahead on a motorway), a logical scenario turns it into parameters with ranges (speeds, gaps, road friction), and a concrete scenario fixes one value for every parameter so that the run can be reproduced exactly. Functional scenarios are derived from hazard analysis and from the operational design domain (the conditions the system is designed to work in), and concrete scenarios are sampled from the logical ranges, either to cover the whole range or to seek out rare, critical combinations, or are reconstructed from recorded incidents. Each concrete scenario is executed with the system under test in the loop, and pass or fail is decided against its expected behaviour, such as no collision, or by criticality measures such as time-to-collision, giving a record of which situations the system handles and which it does not. ISO 34502 gives a scenario-based safety evaluation framework of this kind for automated driving systems on limited-access highways.

example_use_cases.description: A developer of a motorway driving function derives cut-in, cut-out and stopped-vehicle scenarios from its hazard analysis, gives each logical scenario ranges for speeds, gaps and road friction, and runs several thousand sampled concrete scenarios in simulation for every software release, holding back any release in which a run ends in a collision the function was required to avoid.

A robotaxi operator rebuilds the fatal crashes recorded over a decade in the city where it operates as concrete simulation scenarios, and replays each one with its driving system in place of first one human driver and then the other, so that it can show regulators how the system behaves in the crash types that actually occur in its operating area.

An operator of an autonomous passenger ferry tests its collision-avoidance planner on head-on, crossing and overtaking encounters described in the international collision regulations, varying the other vessel's speed, bearing and visibility in a ship simulator, and checks in every run that the ferry keeps its required passing distance and makes the manoeuvre the regulations call for.

limitations.description: The evidence covers only the scenarios that were specified. Real operating conditions cannot be listed exhaustively, so a clean result shows that the system handles the catalogue, not that it is safe; the safety argument depends on how completely the functional scenarios were derived from the hazard analysis and operational design domain, which needs independent review.

Results are only as credible as the simulation. If the models of sensors, vehicle dynamics or other road users have not been validated against the real world, a system can pass in simulation and fail in operation, so key scenarios should be repeated on a test track or against recorded real data.

How concrete scenarios are sampled shapes what the results mean. Covering whole parameter ranges ignores how often each situation occurs, and searching for critical corner cases finds failures efficiently but over-represents rare situations, so neither supports a statement about real-world accident rates unless results are weighted by how often scenarios occur.

Pass criteria encode a judgement about acceptable behaviour. 'No collision' misses near misses and lucky escapes, while criticality measures such as time-to-collision need thresholds that the developer must choose and justify, and the verdicts change with them.

Building scenario catalogues, simulation environments and behaviour models for other road users takes specialist effort and substantial computing. ISO 34502 applies only to limited-access highways, so for urban roads, ships and other domains the scenario structure, pass criteria and coverage argument have to be built without the standard's support.

resources.title: Scenarios for Development, Test and Validation of Automated Vehicles
resources.abstract: The latest version of the ISO 26262 standard from 2016 represents the state of the art for a safety-guided development of safety-critical electric/electronic vehicle systems. These vehicle systems include advanced driver assistance systems and vehicle guidance systems. The development process proposed in the ISO 26262 standard is based upon multiple V-models, and defines activities and work products for each process step. In many of these process steps, scenario based approaches can be applied to achieve the defined work products for the development of automated driving functions. To accomplish the work products of different process steps, scenarios have to focus on various aspects like a human understandable notation or a description via state variables. This leads to contradictory requirements regarding the level of detail and way of notation for the representation of scenarios. In this paper, the authors discuss requirements for the representation of scenarios in different process steps defined by the ISO 26262 standard, propose a consistent terminology based on prior publications for the identified levels of abstraction, and demonstrate how scenarios can be systematically evolved along the phases of the development process outlined in the ISO 26262 standard.
